title: Church Government and Leadership
summary: How Christ rules His church: the offices of elder and deacon, the qualifications for leaders, the main forms of church government, and the role of every member.
description: Who leads the church, and how? This course studies Christ's headship, the New Testament offices of elder (pastor, bishop) and deacon, the qualifications Paul sets out, the episcopal, presbyterian and congregational forms of government, the debate over women in leadership, and the accountability, character and servant-heartedness every church leader needs.
objectives: Explain Christ's headship over the church
Describe the offices of elder and deacon
Study the qualifications for church leaders
Present fairly the main forms of church government
Present fairly the views on women in church leadership
outcomes: Show that elder, bishop and pastor describe one office
List the qualifications in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1
Compare episcopal, presbyterian and congregational government
Apply principles of servant leadership and accountability

modules.title: Christ the Head
modules.intro: The church is not a business or a kingdom of men. This week we see that Christ rules His church, and leaders serve under Him.

lessons.title: One Lord over the church
lessons.body:
God "gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Which is his body" (Ephesians 1:22-23). Christ is "the head of the body, the church... that in all things he might have the preeminence" (Colossians 1:18).

Christ rules His church by His Word and Spirit. Leaders are not owners but stewards (1 Corinthians 4:1-2) and under-shepherds of "the flock of God" (1 Peter 5:2).

This guards against two dangers: leaders who act as if the church belongs to them, and members who ignore Christ's appointed leaders.

lessons.title: Servant leadership
lessons.body:
When the disciples argued about greatness, Jesus said, "ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them... But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister" (Matthew 20:25-26). "Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister" (20:28).

Peter tells elders to lead "not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock" (1 Peter 5:2-3).

Christian leadership is service, example and care, not control, display or profit.

lessons.title: Apostles and the foundation
lessons.body:
The church is "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone" (Ephesians 2:20).

The Twelve and Paul were apostles in a unique sense: eyewitnesses of the risen Christ (Acts 1:21-22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), appointed directly by Him, whose teaching is now preserved in the New Testament.

The word apostle (sent one) is also used more broadly for missionaries such as Barnabas (Acts 14:14). Churches today differ on whether to use the title. All agree that no modern leader has the authority of the original apostles to add to Scripture.

terms.def: Christ's supreme rule over His church.
A manager entrusted with another's property; leaders as stewards of God's people.
Leading by serving others, after Christ's example.
Domineering leadership that Peter forbids (1 Peter 5:3).
One sent; in the unique sense, an eyewitness of the risen Christ appointed by Him.
The apostolic teaching on which the church is built (Ephesians 2:20).

texts.teaches: God gave Christ to be head over all things to the church.
Whoever would be great among you, let him be your servant.
Elders must not be lords over God's heritage but examples to the flock.
It is required in stewards that a man be found faithful.
The church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets.

summary: Christ is the head of the church; leaders are His stewards.
Christian leadership is servant leadership, not domination.
Elders must lead willingly, unselfishly and by example.
The original apostles laid a unique foundation in Scripture.

questions.q: Who is the head of the church?
What did Jesus say about greatness?
What does Peter forbid elders to be?

modules.title: Elders and Deacons
modules.intro: The New Testament describes two ongoing offices in the local church. This week we study elders and deacons.

lessons.title: Elders, bishops and pastors
lessons.body:
The New Testament uses three words for the same leaders:

- **Elder** (presbuteros): stresses maturity.
- **Bishop** or overseer (episkopos): stresses oversight.
- **Pastor** or shepherd (poimen): stresses care and feeding.

Paul called the "elders of the church" of Ephesus and told them the Holy Ghost had made them "overseers, to feed [shepherd] the church of God" (Acts 20:17, 28). In Titus 1:5-7 'elder' and 'bishop' are used of the same office.

Churches in Acts normally had a plurality of elders: Paul "ordained them elders in every church" (Acts 14:23).

lessons.title: The work of elders
lessons.body:
Elders are called to:

- **Teach** sound doctrine and refute error (Titus 1:9; 1 Timothy 5:17).
- **Shepherd** and feed the flock (1 Peter 5:2).
- **Guard** against false teachers, "grievous wolves" (Acts 20:29-31).
- **Pray** for the sick and the flock (James 5:14; Acts 6:4).
- **Lead** and oversee (1 Thessalonians 5:12; Hebrews 13:17).

"Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine" (1 Timothy 5:17). Faithful pastors should be cared for by the church (5:18).

lessons.title: Deacons
lessons.body:
In Acts 6, the apostles were overwhelmed by the daily distribution to widows. They asked the church to choose "seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom" to oversee it, so the apostles could give themselves "to prayer, and to the ministry of the word" (Acts 6:3-4).

The word deacon (diakonos) means servant. Deacons handle practical ministries such as care for the needy, finances and facilities, freeing elders for the Word and prayer.

Paul greets "bishops and deacons" (Philippians 1:1) and gives qualifications for deacons (1 Timothy 3:8-13). Some deacons, like Stephen and Philip, were also powerful in the Word.

terms.def: A mature spiritual leader of a local church.
An overseer; in the New Testament, the same office as elder.
A shepherd who feeds and cares for the flock.
Leadership of a local church by several elders together.
A servant who oversees practical ministries of the church.
The church's recognition and setting apart of a person for office.

texts.teaches: The Holy Ghost made the elders overseers to feed the church of God.
Paul ordained elders in every church.
Elders who rule well deserve double honour.
Choose seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom.
The apostles gave themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.

summary: Elder, bishop and pastor describe one office in the New Testament.
Elders teach, shepherd, guard, pray and lead.
Deacons serve the church's practical needs.
New Testament churches usually had several elders.

questions.q: Which three words describe the same office?
Why were the seven chosen in Acts 6?
options: To oversee care for widows so apostles could pray and preach

questions.q: What do elders who labour in the Word deserve?

modules.title: Qualified to Lead
modules.intro: Paul set out clear qualifications for leaders. This week we study them and how leaders should be chosen and held accountable.

lessons.title: Character before gifting
lessons.body:
"A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach; Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous; One that ruleth well his own house... Not a novice... he must have a good report of them which are without" (1 Timothy 3:2-7; compare Titus 1:6-9).

Almost every quality concerns **character**. Only one, "apt to teach", is a skill. A gifted speaker with poor character is not qualified; a humble, godly, teachable person with sound doctrine is.

lessons.title: Home, money and reputation
lessons.body:
Three areas receive special attention:

- **Home**: "if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?" (1 Timothy 3:5). Faithfulness in marriage and godly parenting matter.
- **Money**: not greedy, not covetous (3:3). Paul warned of those "supposing that gain is godliness" (6:5).
- **Reputation**: "a good report of them which are without" (3:7). Leaders must be trusted by outsiders.

Also, "not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall" (3:6). New converts, however gifted, should not be rushed into leadership.

lessons.title: Choosing and correcting leaders
lessons.body:
Leaders should be tested before serving: "let these also first be proved" (1 Timothy 3:10). "Lay hands suddenly on no man" (5:22).

In Acts the church chose candidates and the apostles appointed them (6:3-6); elders were appointed with prayer and fasting (14:23).

Leaders must also be accountable. "Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses", protecting leaders from false charges. But "Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear" (1 Timothy 5:19-20). Paul even rebuked Peter publicly for hypocrisy (Galatians 2:11-14). No leader is above correction.

terms.def: Having no just charge of wrongdoing against one's life.
Faithful in marriage; literally 'a one-woman man'.
Able to explain and defend sound doctrine.
A recent convert, not yet ready for leadership.
Shameful gain; greed for money.
Being answerable to others for one's conduct and teaching.

texts.teaches: A bishop must be blameless and apt to teach.
One who cannot rule his own house cannot care for the church.
A leader must not be a novice, lest he fall through pride.
Lay hands suddenly on no man.
Leaders who sin should be rebuked before all.

summary: Leadership qualifications are mostly about character.
Home, money and reputation are tested areas.
Leaders should be tested and not appointed hastily.
Leaders are accountable; none is above correction.

questions.q: Which qualification is a skill rather than character?
Why should a novice not be an elder?
How many witnesses are required for an accusation against an elder?
Whom did Paul rebuke publicly in Galatians 2?

modules.title: Forms of Church Government
modules.intro: Christians organise their churches in different ways. This week we compare the main forms fairly and consider women in leadership.

lessons.title: Episcopal and presbyterian
lessons.body:
**Episcopal** government (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Methodist, and many Pentecostal and Nigerian independent churches): authority rests with bishops or overseers above local churches. Some trace this to the apostles' oversight of churches and to Timothy and Titus appointing elders in different cities (Titus 1:5).

**Presbyterian** government (Presbyterian and Reformed churches): each church is led by a body of elders (session), and churches are joined in regional and national councils of elders (presbytery, synod). They point to elders in every church and to the Jerusalem council (Acts 15), where apostles and elders together settled a question for many churches.

lessons.title: Congregational
lessons.body:
**Congregational** government (Baptists and many independent churches): each local church is self-governing under Christ, and the members as a whole have final authority in key decisions such as choosing leaders, receiving members and discipline.

They point to the church choosing the seven (Acts 6:3-5), the whole church disciplining (Matthew 18:17; 1 Corinthians 5:4-5), and letters addressed to whole congregations. Baptist churches cooperate freely in associations and conventions, such as the Nigerian Baptist Convention, without surrendering local autonomy.

Most congregational churches are led by elders or a pastor with deacons, accountable to the members.

lessons.title: Women in church leadership
lessons.body:
Bible-believing Christians differ on whether women may serve as pastors or elders.

**Complementarians** (many Baptist, Reformed and some Pentecostal churches) believe men and women are equal in worth but have different roles, with the office of elder or pastor reserved for qualified men. They cite 1 Timothy 2:12, the qualification "husband of one wife", and the order of creation (2:13).

**Egalitarians** (many Methodist, Pentecostal and charismatic churches) believe all offices are open to gifted women. They cite Galatians 3:28, women prophesying (Acts 2:17; 21:9), Phoebe the deacon (Romans 16:1), Priscilla teaching Apollos (Acts 18:26) and Junia (Romans 16:7), and read 1 Timothy 2 as addressing a local problem.

Both agree women are fully gifted for ministry, and both must honour Scripture.

terms.def: Church government by bishops with authority over several churches.
Church government by elders, joined in regional and national councils.
Church government in which each local church governs itself under Christ.
The self-governance of each local church, held by Baptists.
The view that men and women are equal in worth with distinct roles, elder being for men.
The view that all church offices are open to gifted men and women.

texts.teaches: Titus was left in Crete to ordain elders in every city.
The apostles and elders came together to consider the matter.
The saying pleased the whole multitude, and they chose Stephen and others.
Paul did not permit a woman to teach or usurp authority over a man.
Phoebe was a servant (deacon) of the church at Cenchrea.

summary: Presbyterian: elders lead, joined in councils.
Congregational: each church governs itself under Christ; Baptists cooperate in conventions.
Complementarians and egalitarians differ on women as elders; both value women's ministry.

questions.q: Which form of government do Baptists practise?
Which event do presbyterians cite for councils of elders?
Who was a servant (deacon) of the church at Cenchrea?

options: Equal worth, distinct roles, elder for men
Women may not serve at all

short.q: Show from Scripture that elder, bishop and pastor are one office.
short.model: In Acts 20:17, 28 the elders are called overseers who shepherd the church; Titus 1:5-7 uses elder and bishop for the same office.

short.q: What is servant leadership, according to Jesus?
short.model: Leading by serving others, not dominating as rulers do, following the example of the Son of man who came to serve.

short.q: Why were deacons appointed in Acts 6?
short.model: To oversee the daily distribution to widows so the apostles could give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the Word.
Mostly character: blameless, faithful in marriage, managing the home well, not greedy, not a novice, of good reputation, and able to teach.

short.q: Compare episcopal, presbyterian and congregational government.
short.model: Episcopal: bishops oversee many churches; presbyterian: elders lead, joined in councils; congregational: each local church governs itself under Christ.

short.q: Summarise the complementarian and egalitarian views fairly.
short.model: Complementarians hold equal worth with distinct roles, elder reserved for men (1 Timothy 2); egalitarians hold all offices open to gifted women (Galatians 3:28).

lists.q: List five qualifications for a bishop in 1 Timothy 3.
List three forms of church government.

assignments.title: Leaders after God's heart
assignments.prompt: Using 1 Timothy 3, Titus 1 and 1 Peter 5, write a profile of a godly church leader. Then identify three common failures of church leaders today and show from Scripture how they can be prevented.

assignments.title: How my church is governed
assignments.prompt: Describe how your church or denomination is governed. Identify which form it follows, explain its biblical basis, and evaluate its strengths and possible weaknesses in the light of this course.

reading: Chad Owen Brand and R. Stanton Norman (eds), Perspectives on Church Government: Five Views
James R. Beck (ed.), Two Views on Women in Ministry
